title: On-prem / Air-gapped: GPU drivers, offline licensing & artifact delivery deep dive
summary: SE-led deep dive on on-prem air-gapped deployment: artifact delivery options, offline licensing activation, GPU driver compatibility and runtime performance tradeoffs (KV caching, batching, quantization). Agreed next steps for delivering signed artifact bundle, run a short on-prem benchmark, and schedule driver validation window.
topics: artifact delivery - signed bundles, checksums, GPG
offline licensing - time-limited license files, activation process
GPU drivers - supported CUDA/CuDNN, driver signing, kernel modules
runtime performance - KV cache warmup, batching strategies, quantization impact
security controls - HSM/KMS, audit logs, SSO considerations
action_items: Maya Chen: prepare signed artifact bundle (tar + GPG + sha256) and upload transfer instructions by 2027-04-09
Ramon Patel: provide offline licensing activation steps, sample license file format, and license validator CLI by 2027-04-09
Liam O'Connor: confirm target on-prem node spec (GPU model, kernel version) and source a test machine by 2027-04-12
Priya Raj: allocate 2 hours next week for driver compatibility test window (suggest 2027-04-14)
Ellen Wu: provide list of compliance questions to attach to ticket by 2027-04-08
next_steps: Redwood to deliver artifact bundle over secure transfer method with GPG and checksums
Customer to confirm exact GPU and kernel versions so SE can validate driver build
Schedule 2-hour driver validation and small-scale latency/throughput run
Redwood to share short benchmark script and expected metrics for 1k token synthetic workload
Set follow-up call after tests to review results and scope pilot
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for blocking time. We wanted to dig into the on-prem air-gapped delivery flow, GPU driver expectations, offline license activation, and then some runtime knobs like KV cache and batching. Ramon will drive the technical pieces.
[00:00:12] Ramon Patel: Hey, thanks. Quick agenda — artifact packaging and verification, license file activation, driver and kernel constraints, then performance tuning notes. Also Q and A.
[00:00:25] Dinesh Kapoor: Sounds good. Our key constraints are strict air gap, company policy requires signed artifacts, and we need to ensure compatibility with a mix of A100 and A30 nodes across two datacenters.
[00:00:38] Ramon Patel: Got it. For artifacts we produce a signed bundle: tarball with runtime binaries, model artifacts and a signed license binary. We sign with GPG and generate sha256 checksums. For air-gapped customers we also provide an encrypted USB image option and step-by-step import instructions.
[00:00:58] Priya Raj: When you say signed, is that an internal Redwood key or do you provide a way for us to re-sign?
[00:01:05] Ramon Patel: Primary signing is with Redwood's GPG key to ensure integrity end-to-end. We can provide the public key for verification. If you require re-signing with your own key during ingestion, we can support that as an additional verification step but we typically recommend verifying Redwood's signature before re-signing.
[00:01:18] Liam O'Connor: How do we get the keys into the air-gapped environment securely?
[00:01:22] Maya Chen: We usually exchange over a couriered USB with tamper-evident packaging and share checksums out-of-band. For very regulated customers we can also provide an HSM-wrapped license that the customer activates with a one-time code.
[00:01:36] Ellen Wu: On the license piece, we need to understand exactly what telemetry or callbacks occur. Nothing should phone home from an air-gapped node.
[00:01:44] Ramon Patel: Understood. Our offline license activation is purely local — the license file is a signed blob that the runtime validates locally using the provided public key. No outbound network calls are required. The only optional component is for activation help where a support engineer could generate a time-limited key for you, but that can be done via secure courier or a managed key transfer.
[00:02:03] Dinesh Kapoor: Good. Now drivers: we run RHEL 8.9 with 5.14 kernels on most nodes. A100s are on 470.x driver in some racks and 515.x in others, long story. What's the recommended driver surface?
[00:02:16] Ramon Patel: Our runtime supports CUDA 11.8 through 12.3 in the tested matrix, and we build driver-shim packages for 470+, 510+, and 515+. The critical part is matching the right NVML and libcudart versions; we publish a compatibility table. If you have 470.x we can provide a specific driver bundle; if you upgrade to 515 we can provide the newer bundle. We also support containerized runtime that talks to host driver via nvidia-container-runtime.
[00:02:42] Priya Raj: Any kernel module signing requirements? We have strict kmod signing policies and Secure Boot enabled.
[00:02:48] Ramon Patel: We sign our kernel modules with a key that you can enroll into MOK. For Secure Boot environments we provide the signing certificate and instructions to enroll via mokutil. For extreme cases you can run our runtime inside a VM that avoids some of the host kernel constraints, but that adds overhead.
[00:03:02] Liam O'Connor: For our testing we want to validate throughput and tail latency for our typical prompt lengths — usually 512 tokens average. Can you share the benchmark script?
[00:03:11] Ramon Patel: Yes, we'll share a small synthetic harness that runs single-node and multi-threaded loads. It also exercises KV caching warmup. Note that KV cache warmup behavior matters a lot for latency — cold-starts will be slower. For your workload we recommend an initial warm-up phase or prefix caching if the prompts are similar.
[00:03:29] Dinesh Kapoor: TL;DR on quantization: does Redwood recommend int8 or int4 for production?
[00:03:33] Ramon Patel: Tradeoffs: int8 gives the best cost/perf without large quality loss for most models, int4 can reduce memory and inference cost more aggressively but needs model-specific calibration and you will likely see small degradation on certain tasks. We provide quantized model variants and a quality evaluation harness so you can run regressions against your eval set. For financial NLU tasks we often recommend starting with int8 and running an A/B.
[00:03:54] Ellen Wu: Is there any difference in driver requirements for int8 quantized kernels?
[00:03:58] Ramon Patel: Not really different on the driver side; it's more about our runtime selecting optimized kernels and fused ops. But some of the GPU tensor core paths are faster on CUDA 12.x, so where possible we suggest newer CUDA for peak throughput.
[00:04:12] Speaker 6: Quick question, what about KV cache sizing? If we have many concurrent sessions do you use a shared cache?
[00:04:18] Ramon Patel: We support a multi-tenant KV cache per node with configurable eviction policies. For on-prem you can tune the cache size based on GPU memory and expected active session count. If you need hard isolation, you can pin customers to dedicated pools.
[00:04:32] Maya Chen: To ground this — for a single A100 80GB with int8 and batching 8 we often see X throughput and 95th percentile latency of Y on our bench. Ramon, can you put approximate numbers for 512-token prompts?
[00:04:46] Ramon Patel: Roughly for a 512-token prompt on an A100 80GB, with int8 and batch size 8, you should expect sustained throughput ~180-220 tokens/sec and p95 latency in the 220-350 ms range per token depending on prompt complexity and kv warm state. Those are ballpark; we'll include a table.
[00:05:04] Dinesh Kapoor: That helps. Also, in air-gapped mode how are model updates handled? Do we pull incremental patches or full re-deploy?
[00:05:11] Ramon Patel: We support delta model patches for some quant formats, but for safety we usually deliver a full model bundle for major releases. Patch updates can be provided as diffs if you want smaller transfers — those are signed as well.
[00:05:22] Priya Raj: We need an auditor-friendly install log for the runbooks.
[00:05:26] Ramon Patel: The installer emits a deterministic install log including checksums, GPG verification records, driver install status, and license activation record. We also include a machine-readable audit file you can ingest to your SIEM.
[00:05:36] Liam O'Connor: About the license file format, can you describe fields?
[00:05:39] Ramon Patel: It's a signed JSON blob containing customer id, license type, expiration, allowed models, node count, and a signature. For air-gapped installs the runtime validates the signature locally. We provide a CLI validator so you can pre-check licenses before applying.
[00:05:53] Ellen Wu: Any PII in those blobs? We want minimal exposure.
[00:05:57] Ramon Patel: No PII. Only tenant id and policy fields.
[00:06:00] Maya Chen: Ok, let's talk artifact transport options briefly. 1) Encrypted USB with tamper evidence and GPG-signed tarball, 2) customer-provided shuttle with presigned transfer token to a temporary S3 endpoint that you download into a controlled environment before ingest, 3) physical courier with checksum via a second channel. Which do you prefer?
[00:06:16] Liam O'Connor: Probably encrypted USB for the first run. We can evaluate the shuttle later.
[00:06:19] Dinesh Kapoor: Could you include a small smoke test that runs post-install to validate driver and runtime?
[00:06:24] Ramon Patel: Yes, the bundle includes a smoke.sh that validates driver presence, nvml, runs a single inference and validates outputs against a hash.
[00:06:33] Priya Raj: For the driver test window, what do you need from us?
[00:06:36] Ramon Patel: Node access details, kernel and driver versions, and preferred time window. We'll provide a checklist. The test is non-disruptive but we ask that you isolate a test machine.
[00:06:44] Maya Chen: Let's capture next steps: we'll send the artifact bundle and license samples, Ramon will include the smoke test and benchmark script, Liam to confirm node specs and book test window.
[00:06:55] Dinesh Kapoor: Works for me. One more question on rollbacks: if a model deploy causes issues can we fallback to previous model locally without contacting Redwood?
[00:07:02] Ramon Patel: Yes, we support pinned model versions and local rollbacks. The runtime keeps a small cache of previous model files depending on disk space policy, and you can configure automatic rollback on error.
[00:07:12] Ellen Wu: Anything we should watch for in terms of licensing compliance if we rollback frequently?
[00:07:16] Ramon Patel: License counts are enforced at runtime and tied to active node count and model type; rolling back doesn't change counts unless you activate a different license. We will document the guidance.
[00:07:25] Maya Chen: Ok thanks all. We'll follow up with the bundles and proposed dates.
[00:07:29] Liam O'Connor: Thanks, appreciate it.
[00:07:31] Ramon Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll put the artifacts in motion.
[00:07:35] Maya Chen: Meeting adjourned.
